Our group has spent the past year or so playing D&D using the 5e rules but playing with a more traditional D&D mentality. Over the course of this time, we have come up with a number of house rules to help encourage this play style. I thought I might share them here as a series of posts. I certainly don't mean to imply that our style of play is the One True Way, but if you are looking for a more traditional experience, you might find these rules helpful.

In the original D&D game (as well as basic and advanced varieties), monsters are deadly, and you are often better off avoiding them than fighting them. This is especially true of wandering monsters, which typically do not have much treasure. In our campaigns, treasure from wandering monsters comes from the pocket change table in the DMG, and treasure from monsters in their lairs is rolled on the Hoard tables. Obviously, players will want to target the treasure in monster lairs, avoiding as many wandering monsters as possible. Smart players will also find a way to avoid (or trick) monsters in their lairs as well.

To give players extra incentive to seek out monster lairs and to avoid wandering monsters, we do experience a little differently than is suggested in the 5e books. We award experience points for defeating monsters as well as for winning non-magical treasure – including coinage, gems, art objects, and trade goods. The party receives experience points equal to 100 times the sum of the challenge ratings of all defeated monsters. They also receives 1 experience point for every 1 gold piece of non-magical treasure brought back to town. Monetary awards from NPCs also grant experience points at this rate. Experience is divided equally among players with each NPC earning a half share.

The 100 exp/CR rule is intended to be reminiscent of Gary's 100 exp/hp rule from Men & Magic. Gary later described this rate of experience as way too high, but we find it works well in 5e. I ran the math on 1 exp/gp (happy to share this if there is interest), and this rule will break down around level 17. At this level, players will accumulate experience points from treasure too quickly. Given that none of us have reached level 17 since circa the late 1980s, this is not a major concern for any of us.

I know that many dungeon masters award experience points for reaching story goals or else just level everyone up when a goal is met. We tend to run exclusively sandbox games, so this method does not work for us. As players, we expect to have free reign over where our characters go and what they do. If the DM rewards certain objectives and not others, it leaves a bad taste in our mouths.

I like to keep physical gains separate from mental ones. Cheaters get gold but the earnest become strong, and that's how I like to mold my DnD rewards.

Experience is earned from 1-100, where you level up at 100. If a fight was easy then the players earn about about 10 exp, hard fights may be closer to 35, and exactly how much they earn or how hard they fought was up to the DM's discretion.

The physical gains (swords, gold, magic stuff) do not change based off of how hard the fight was. I don't like rewarding someone who tricks a dragon into killing himself the same thing as someone who actually killed the dragon. You can cheat for your gold, but experience should always be earned with hard work.

Few things to add balance to this kind of system: Experience over 100 is halved and then added to the next level. Experience earned is based off of the median level of the party. Players under this level earn double experience. Players over this level earn half.

If I were to play a campaign focused around thieves, I'd definitely consider coming back to your post and stealing some of your ideas. And I might use your system for items that have personal value to a character (a history book of a specific type of magic for a wizard, a totem of a barbarian's clan, etc.). Thanks for the ideas, man.
